title: Observability playback runbook for change reviewers
author: Ravi Kapoor
content:
Overview:
This runbook describes the 'observability playback' workflow for reviewers who approve configuration or code changes that impact runtime telemetry, routing, batching, and model-serving surface area. The goal is to give change reviewers a repeatable, low-friction process to validate that a change: preserves SLOs, does not inject cost-regressing behavior, and does not widen error budgets.

Who should use this document:
- Change reviewers for infra and platform PRs that touch telemetry, routing, batching, cache, or model-serving subsystems.
- SREs and platform engineers responsible for rollout approval.
- Oncall leads validating post-deploy behavior during canaries.

Why a playback is important:
- Production traces and metrics are often non-deterministic; a structured playback lets reviewers reliably compare before/after using the same stimulus.
- Detects regressions introduced by compiler/kernel swaps, quantization rollouts, prefetch changes, and routing policy updates.

Scope and release types covered:
- Applies to changes that affect request path behavior (e.g., allocator/eviction policy, batching, kernel selection, model variant routing, prefetch rules, telemetry sampling).
- Recommended for all canary and small-batch rollouts; mandatory for changes that alter SLI computation or token-cost attribution.

Prerequisites and quick checklist before starting playback:
1) Access: reviewer has access to the target environment (canary/preview) and dashboard snapshot tools.
2) Baseline snapshot: capture a dashboard snapshot (or export) from the last 72 hours.
3) Synthetic workload harness: know which synthetic tenant(s) or workload profiles to use (see table below).
4) Runbook owner: designate an operator and a rollback owner for the session.

Table: Standard synthetic workload profiles (copy into your lab script)
| Profile name | Description | Representative tenant | Target QPS | Typical seq len | Purpose |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| small-chat | Short-chat model path, 8–16 tokens prefix | tenant-sim:chat-small | 50 qps | 64 | Latency & tail-latency smoke test |
| shopping-browse | Multi-turn with embeddings and rerank | tenant-sim:shopping | 20 qps | 128 | Batching and KV cache coverage |
| long-context | 2k+ token end-to-end | tenant-sim:long | 2 qps | 2048 | Memory/KV stress and kernel selection |

Playback session step-by-step procedure:
1) Prepare baseline artifacts (30–45 minutes)
   a. Export current dashboards for the services touched by the change (CPU/GPU utilization, token-per-second, request latencies p50/p95/p99, error rate). Save as baseline snapshot with timestamp and PR id.
   b. Note recent SLO burn rates and outstanding incidents. If error budget for the component > 10% burn in last 7d, escalate to SRE manager before proceeding.

2) Configure the synthetic harness (5–10 minutes)
   a. Choose the synthetic profile(s) from the table. For model-serving tuners, always include "shopping-browse" to exercise batching and embedding paths.
   b. Set the harness to run replay for 10 minutes at target QPS, with the same request headers and metadata used in production routing (tenant ID, priority tag).

3) Baseline run (10–15 minutes)
   a. Run the harness against the current (pre-change) canary environment or a snapshot clone.
   b. Record: traces (sampled 1 in 10), flamegraphs of top kernels, and aggregated metric export (CSV).
   c. Save artifacts under /tmp/playbacks/<PR_ID>/baseline/<timestamp>/ .

4) Deploy change to canary (operator)
   a. Deploy the patch behind the canary gate. Ensure feature flags are scoped to the canary cohort.
   b. Wait for health checks to pass (default: 3 consecutive successful health probes at 5s intervals).

5) Post-change run (10–15 minutes)
   a. Run the same synthetic harness with identical parameters against the post-change canary.
   b. Collect the same set of artifacts (traces, flamegraphs, metric CSVs).

6) Automated diff snapshot and quick checks (5 minutes)
   a. Run the included comparator script: scripts/observability_playback/compare.py --baseline <path> --candidate <path> --out <summary.json>. The script derives per-metric percent change, P95 delta, and a kernel-usage diff.
   b. Quick fail-fast thresholds (if any triggered, stop and investigate):
      - p95 latency increase >= 15% for small-chat or shopping-browse profiles.
      - error rate increase >= 0.1 percentage points absolute or 50% relative, whichever is lower.
      - GPU utilization increase > 20% at equal QPS (indicates cost regression).

7) Deep dive (15–30 minutes) if quick checks flag anomalies
   a. Use trace links to compare top slow spans and the associated kernel names (e.g., attention-fused-kernel-v2, kv-restore-path).
   b. Check batching histograms: average batch size, batch wait time. If batch size decreased > 20% with same QPS, consider batching misconfiguration.
   c. Inspect KV cache hit-rate delta. If hit-rate drops by > 10% and latency increases, investigate prefix-routing or cache-invalidation paths.

8) Decide: approve / soft-fail / rollback
   - Approve: no thresholds breached and no unexplained kernel regressions; add a one-line approval comment to PR and annotate the playback artifacts.
   - Soft-fail (monitor longer): minor regressions (p95 < 15% and GPU delta < 10%) — require extended canary (2× duration) and a monitoring ticket assigned to the change author.
   - Rollback: any of the following:
     * p95 increase >= 30% or absolute p95 > target p95 SLO (see SLOs section)
     * error-rate spike above automated alerting threshold (see Alerts)
     * cost/GPU regression > 30% at same QPS

Important SLOs and thresholds (use these as quick references)
- Generate request p99 (inference path): target < 800ms, alert page if > 1200ms sustained for > 5 minutes.
- Successful response rate: target 99.9% (0.1% tolerated), alert if < 99.5% over 10 minutes.
- Batch wait time p95: target < 30ms for interactive profiles; alert if > 100ms.
- KV cache hit rate: target >= 85% for production cohorts; flag if < 75%.

Alerting and escalation map (compact)
- Pager: inference-core-oncall (primary) -> SRE lead (secondary) -> Platform eng manager (tertiary).
- Cost or GPU regression: paging-hotline-finance (notify) + infra-cost-team slack channel.
- Observability playback failures (scripts/compare exceptions): file ticket with logs and tag observability-team.

Artifacts and where to store them
- Dashboard snapshot export: saved to /artifacts/playbacks/<PR_ID>/dashboard-snapshots.zip
- Trace exports and sampling map: /artifacts/playbacks/<PR_ID>/traces/
- Comparator output JSON: /artifacts/playbacks/<PR_ID>/compare-summary.json
- Add links to PR as a checklist item with the artifacts attached.

Automation helpers and recommended scripts
- scripts/observability_playback/collect_metrics.sh
- scripts/observability_playback/trace_exporter.py --service inference-core --since <ts> --out <path>
- scripts/observability_playback/compare.py (produces CSV and JSON summaries)
- Jenkins job: "obs-playback-runner" can run a reproducible job with parameters PR_ID, PROFILE, DURATION. The job archives artifacts to the artifacts bucket.

Common failure modes and investigation pointers:
- Symptom: higher kernel time but same batch size.
  Investigation: inspect kernel version mapping in runtime-annotations; check for JIT/kernels swapped in the compilation layer.
- Symptom: batch wait times increased but GPU utilization decreased.
  Investigation: look at connection churn or client-side rate shaping; verify queuing/backpressure metrics.
- Symptom: KV hit-rate collapse after change.
  Investigation: confirm cache key serialization compatibility; check whether a migration/eviction policy was changed.

Post-session notes and hygiene:
1) Record the session outcome in the PR: link artifacts and summarize breaches or concerns.
2) If extended canary required, set explicit monitoring windows (start/end times) and assign the monitoring ticket with SLAs.
3) Add a short retrospective note to the "observability-playbacks" daily log (location: /team-logs/observability-playbacks.md) if the change required deep dive.

Appendix A - Example compare command and sample output
$ python scripts/observability_playback/compare.py --baseline /tmp/playbacks/PR-123/baseline --candidate /tmp/playbacks/PR-123/candidate --out /tmp/playbacks/PR-123/summary.json
Sample summary.json (abridged human-readable):
- p95_latency_change_percent: 8.2
- p99_latency_change_percent: 4.5
- error_rate_change_abs_percent: 0.02
- gpu_util_change_percent: 5.1
- top_kernel_shift: attention-fused-kernel-v1 -> attention-fused-kernel-v2

Appendix B - Safety checklist (must sign-off before approving change)
- [ ] Baseline artifacts captured and attached.
- [ ] Synthetic harness used matches production routing metadata.
- [ ] Comparator ran without exceptions and results stored.
- [ ] An owner is assigned for extended monitoring if needed.
- [ ] Rollback owner identified and has permission to execute rollback.

Notes and future improvements (open items):
- Integrate playback runner with canary automation so baseline vs candidate runs are executed automatically as part of the canary pipeline.
- Add automatic delta-alerting to PR when comparator shows p95 change > 10% so reviewers receive early feedback.
- Expand synthetic profile catalog with more multimodal scenarios (vision+text).
